input: This tutorial passage explains the pump affinity laws, which are a set of simple and highly useful relationships that describe how the performance of a centrifugal pump changes when its speed is varied. Understanding these relationships is valuable because they allow the behaviour of the pump at one speed to be related, in a straightforward way, to its expected behaviour at another speed. The affinity laws consist of three proportionalities. First, the flow varies in direct proportion to the speed: as the speed increases, the flow increases in line with it. Secondly, the head varies with the square of the speed, so a change in speed produces a more pronounced change in the head that the pump generates. Thirdly, the power varies with the cube of the speed, which means that the power requirement responds even more strongly to a change in speed than either the flow or the head. A simple worked check helps to make this point clear. If the speed is doubled, the power is multiplied by 8. This striking result follows directly from the third proportionality and illustrates why even moderate changes in pump speed can have such a significant effect on power demand. Overall, the three proportionalities together provide a compact summary of how flow, head and power each respond when the speed of a centrifugal pump is changed. It is also worth emphasising that the laws are most helpful when they are considered together rather than in isolation. A change of speed does not alter only one aspect of pump performance; it alters the flow, the head and the power at the same time, each in its own proportion. Keeping the three relationships together gives a much fuller picture of what a proposed speed change actually involves for the pump and for the equipment that drives it.
target: The pump affinity laws state how a centrifugal pump responds to a change of speed, and the outcome for power is the sharpest of the three: doubling the speed multiplies the power by 8. The laws are three proportionalities. Flow is proportional to speed. Head is proportional to the square of the speed. Power is proportional to the cube of the speed. Each law compares the same pump at two speeds, with the geometry unchanged, and each quantity takes its own exponent. Flow follows the speed directly, because the volume displaced per unit time scales with how fast the impeller turns. Head follows the square, because the velocity imparted to the liquid scales with speed and the head follows the square of that velocity. Power follows the cube, because it combines the flow scaling with the head scaling in a single product. The worked check is the cube law read at a doubling. Twice the speed gives twice the flow at four times the head, and the power, as the product of the two, rises by the full factor stated at the outset. The three proportionalities should be applied as a set. Using the flow law alone gives the new duty rate but not the new duty point pressure or the new load on the driver. The affinity laws describe the pump itself under a speed change; they state how its characteristic quantities move together when speed is the only variable altered. The exponents also explain why speed is such a strong control variable for a pump. A modest increase in speed buys flow at a moderate rate, head at a faster rate, and a power bill at the fastest rate of all. Conversely, a modest reduction in speed gives up flow slowly while shedding power quickly. That asymmetry is the practical content of the affinity laws, and it follows from the exponents alone, without any property of a particular pump beyond the laws themselves. The same pump, the same liquid and the same geometry are assumed throughout; the laws compare speeds, and only speeds.
